segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

hard_spots.why_hard: 坊や is used repeatedly to and of a child stated to be a girl (p2 女の子). Literal 'boy / sonny' would mislead English readers about sex; neutralising to 'baby' loses period usage. Needs consistent policy plus margin note, not silent resolution.

Potato is hard, gritty ざくざく, tasteless, as if frozen 凍ったかのやうに. Must stay literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything; English will want to explain it as symbol of poverty or psychology. The detachment (心が淋しくうつむく) happens inside the mouthful without commentary.

Long looping sentences of abstract nouns:善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびも; なつかしみと許し; 安らかさ / 安息. Who the three are, when this day is (old age, death, time itself), and whether 安息 is religious must not be clarified. English pressure to vary synonyms, ennoble, or call it heaven/premonition/daydream must be resisted; keep plain repetition.

うまうまうまうま with spoon banged down while looking at mother. Onomatopoeic yummy-yummy babble, not lexical sentence. Transcribe effect without making child articulate; keep physical simultaneity with mother's 坊や call.

Author glosses: 卓テーブル, 怜悧れいり, 微笑ほほゑみ, 茫然ぼんやり, 希のぞみ etc. in historical kanaづかひ. Readings fix sense (テーブル as table, ほほゑみ as smile). English cannot show ruby; do not italicise into exoticism. 卓 vs テーブル shift and food vessels (茶碗, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 藍色の深い鍋) carry poor-household period texture to keep concrete.

Ending refuses arc:箸をおいた, resolve to work and rise early, child put to breast falls asleep mid-feed, room goes still, man stands still and whispers 嵐だな. No moral, no consolation gloss. Must allow eternal and next morning to sit side by side; last line only weather, echoing p1 and p19 without symbolism.

motifs.english: Keep one plain English set throughout and repeat, not vary: quiet / quietly for 静か, restful / restfulness for 安らかさ, rest/repose for 安息. Same vocabulary for evening, mother's manner, and vision so table and eternity share language. Do not lift into lyricism or religious peace.
motifs.why: Connective tissue binding supper, memory and vision; fluent English will vary into calm/peaceful/serene/still and destroy network.

motifs.english: Keep far / distant / far-off for 遠い, not remote/removed/estranged. Preserve spatialising of time: future seen through bottom of eyes as distant picture.
motifs.why: Marks mother's detachment: gaze, heart and future all go far. Ordinary usage made deliberate by recurrence; unifies potato moment and vision.

motifs.english: Keep silently / without speaking for 黙って, not wordlessly/tacitly in variation. Her silence is plot: husband asks twice why she is quiet.
motifs.why: From shared smiling silence at table to trance silence to unreported vision; must track as same word.

motifs.english: Keep smile / smiling for 微笑, 笑ひ, ゑみ, ほほゑみ as one field; allow smile overflowed / held back as text has it. Same smiles on parents and on vision figures.
motifs.why: Tenderness and vision share lexis: parents' helpless overflowing smiles and the three figures' continuous quiet smiles. Varying into grin/beam delights would break link.

motifs.english: Keep weariness, sadness, suffering (and trouble/anguish なやみ where present) as fixed equivalents and keep lists long with and…and. Do not compress lists or substitute hardship/pain synonyms.
motifs.why: Recurrence across body, memory and vision is the argument: same burdens at table, in past three years, and inside endless story. Text power is accumulation, not striking phrase.

motifs.english: Keep fond remembrance (or nostalgic fondness if chosen) for なつかしみ and forgiveness for 許し as paired fixed nouns wherever they occur; never paraphrase into nostalgia/pardon/reconciliation variants.
motifs.why: Paired nouns on which whole vision turns; past suffering remembered as なつかしい夢, future all turned into なつかしみと許し. Destroying repetition destroys crux.

motifs.english: Keep storm for 嵐 and sound of rain-wind for 雨風の音 as sound heard, forgotten, heard again. Do not turn into symbolism or pathetic fallacy; weather simply goes on outside.
motifs.why: Frame: p1 heard, p8 unheard through bustle, p19 quietly heard in silence, p38 whispered when still. Must remain arc of sound.

motifs.english: Keep drifting markers as at some point / before she knew it / suddenly for いつか, いつとなく, ふと without firming into she realised / she imagined. Preserve soft transitions where present, memory and future soak into one another.
motifs.why: Medium of story: she slides rather than decides; she feels as if grown old over three years. Signposting would rationalise consciousness that experiences time as unbroken telling.

motifs.english: Keep three years / only three years / only a little while as literal arithmetic shock, repeated plainly. Do not inflate into years of hardship moral.
motifs.why: Felt lifetime versus counted three years is pivot from vision back to resolve to work; repetition carries hope that is not improvement but distant holding.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for supper and memory, allowing the vision's gnomic present-future (p17 過去るであらう…変る事だらう) to stay timeless without shifting whole text into present. Do not use historical present to enliven domestic opening or to signal meditation as important.
narration.frame: Single evening: outside the door a storm; inside a narrow room under a dim lamp hanging by the wall, young parents and plump baby at table for supper. Narration begins jointly on couple watching child, narrows almost imperceptibly via potato into mother, stays mostly inside her drifting attention, returns to shared dialogue and closing tableau of clearing, nursing, stillness, weather.
narration.narrator: Third-person literary narrator, close and gentle, starting omniscient-joint then settling near the mother without explicit interior marking; often leaves who-sees and when soft. Vision never reported to husband; husband's questions and plain answers stay outside it.
narration.person: third person, sliding focus from couple to mother
narration.tense_habits: Japanese mixes てゐた progressive-past and た completion with nonpast/gnomic だらう in reflection; stative weariness and continuing smiles rendered as ongoing states. Historical kana and ruby aid reading but do not change tense. English should allow long looping and… and… sentences and slow lists to pool, not shorten into crisp modern periods.
timeline: p1: outside door, already dark, violent rain-wind, storm
p2-p9: supper begins; baby gripping table snatches so bowls/pots moved underneath leaving spoon and small plate; noisy happy feeding in snatches; storm forgotten
p10-p13: mother serves beef/onion/carrot/potato from dark-blue pot, tastes gritty tasteless potato as if frozen; heart turns lonely, recalls poor sad three married years as dreamlike

p14-p18: arithmetic (only about three years) versus feeling grown old; drifting into dim picture of three quiet people heads together over endless story, smiling unmoving, wrapped in remembrance/forgiveness/rest
p19-p20: husband asks why silent (first time); she starts, cannot say it, hears storm quietly, holds thought that day of remembrance/forgiveness/rest after long life/sadness/suffering exists

p21-p32: husband asks again; she answers only banal startling fact of short marriage and vague great hope; he answers it won't be much longer, child will walk; baby cries うまうま, fed; chopsticks laid down
p33-p38: resolve to work, rise early tomorrow; child put to breast falls asleep cheek to breast; room still; man stands still and whispers storm

body.say: Hold vision unlocated and diction plain; let eternal and next morning sit side by side. Repeat abstract nouns, do not explain potato or husband, do not end on moral.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Annotate only what sentence cannot give: 坊や usage for a girl, aluminium pot / dark-blue pot period poverty without picturesque gloss, historical kana/ruby where sense depends on gloss, baby babble. Never annotate what context supplies; never use note to resolve vision's three figures or day into heaven/old age/death.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taisho literary prose, gentle slightly formal but plain in its own terms; power in accumulation and recurrence, not striking phrases. Allow long looping sentences and slow lists of everything life contains. Tenderness rendered physically (cheek pinched, rice pushed into two mouths, cheek to breast) not named grandly. Do not ennoble food or poverty, do not coarsen husband's warmth, do not lift vision into lyric consolation.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No surnames or given names in text; do not invent. Keep kin labels as common nouns (father/mother/husband/wife) where narrator uses them. For 坊や do not use Boy/Sonny; use baby / little one with margin note on period generic, pending editor decision, and keep consistent. No Sensei or honorifics to preserve. Name order not applicable.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Nothing kept in Japanese in reading view except defended need: transcribe baby うまうまうまうま as uma-uma with note rather than translating yummy, if editor allows; otherwise plain yummy-yummy babble. Food 御飯 as rice, 茶碗/土瓶/鍋 as bowls/pots in English; do not leave Japanese vessels untranslated.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese uses 『』 for direct speech (きかない奴だな, どうして黙ってるの, 坊や, うまうま, etc.) and embedded thought/独言. Render direct speech in English double quotes, baby babble likewise, with plain dialogue tags. Do not add said-softeners or resolve unattributed speakers where text leaves soft.
style_sheet.register: Narrator: plain gentle literary slightly formal, past-default, long periodic where Japanese loops. Husband speech rough-edged warm masculine colloquial (なァ, 俺たち, 奴, 独言-like strength) without dialect costume or archaism. Wife speech soft feminine period polite (ませんのね, んですものね, ませうね) audible as feminine-polite, not coy. Baby: noise, not lexis.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby gives reading/nuance: 卓テーブル, 怜悧れいり, 微笑ほほゑみ, 茫然ぼんやり, 希のぞみ. Follow gloss sense (table, perspicacious, smile, blankly, hope) in English body; do not italicise or footnote ruby itself unless sense genuinely ambiguous. Italics reserved for emphasis present in sense, not for foreignism.

head.reason: Both name the same crux: an unexplained temporal reversal, triggered by the potato, in which three years feel like an aged lifetime yet appear dear and forgiven from an immense distance, continuously interrupted by the ordinary supper. Option 1's emphasis on repeated words and drifting syntax describes how that reversal is enacted, not a different crux, while Option 0's fuller account also preserves the unresolved ending and the husband's partial response.
head.say: Same crux - Option 0 and Option 1 name the same thing; my pick is Option 0. Both readers identify the unexplained temporal reversal triggered by the potato, in which three years feel like a whole aged life yet look dear and forgiven from an immense distance, held inside and interrupted by the ordinary supper. Option 1's repetition and drifting syntax are how that reversal works in the language, not a different crux; Option 0 states the whole movement more completely, including the unresolved return to work and the husband meeting it only partway. House log: The two crux statements converge, so Option 0 goes forward without a fork.

crux.for_the_english: Do not clarify the vision into a daydream about old age, a religious consolation, or a resolution to endure. Keep its tense, distance and agency vague, its key words unvaried, and do not soften the nearness of that peace to death. The mother must be allowed to find the present already becoming sweet from an imagined afterwards, then to return without the story explaining her.
crux.point: The frozen, tasteless potato opens a temporal reversal: three years of married poverty feel like a whole aged life, yet seen from a far future they already look like a dear, forgiven dream.
crux.why: In p11-14 a badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, coldly flavourless — detaches the mother from supper. She recalls tears, want and sickness, feels suddenly old, then corrects herself: it has been only about three years. In p16-20 that detachment becomes the still picture of three people telling an endless story containing all good, evil, sorrow and anger, while simply smiling; everything will change into なつかしみ and 許し only once life has passed. Her silence at the table, and the husband twice asking why she is silent, is the action of the story.

crux.for_the_english: Preserve the repeated words and the long, drifting periods in the interior passages, even where fluent English would vary, shorten or connect them. Keep plain words plain — quiet, far, smile, sorrow, suffering, dear/longed-for, forgiveness, peace — rather than ennobling them. Let noisy scene and motionless vision remain syntactically unlike.
crux.point: That reversal is carried by incantatory repetition and unbroken, drifting sentences set against the baby's noisy, abruptly broken supper scene.
crux.why: From p12 on, 静か, 遠い, 悲しみ, 苦しみ, なつかしみ, 許し and 安らかさ recur in long chains, often with little logical tightening; p20 and p28 repeat days, years and 'after' until time itself blurs. Around it the child bangs a spoon, shouts うまうま, is fed in haste (p5-9, p29-32), and dialogue is short. If the repetitions are treated as redundancy and the vision is made concise and lyrical, its trance — and the mother's absence from the room — disappears.

second.say:
Confidence: high that these two, together, are where this text stands or falls; the temporal pivot is explicit in the three-years correction, and the lexical repetitions are pervasive rather than incidental.
What would change my mind: evidence from Shizu's other work or from period usage that なつかしみ/許し/安らかさ carried a fixed religious meaning here, which would make a more doctrinal English rendering faithful rather than clarifying.

body.why: The 38-paragraph story totals only about 3,400 characters with no chapters or scene breaks, so the whole supper scene holds in one reading as a single part.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the vision unlocated, unbelabored, and in the same plain diction as the supper. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, a daydream, or a premonition, and do not make the three figures explicitly the couple grown old. Let abstract nouns repeat rather than finding synonyms for them: quiet/rest/peace, nostalgia or fond remembrance, forgiveness, sadness, suffering, weariness. The English will want to vary, explain, and lift these into lyricism; resist that ennoblement.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on a change of temporal distance inside an ordinary mouthful, and on that change not being explained. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless, “as if frozen” — detaches the young mother from the table and lets the three years of her marriage look first like a whole lifetime already lived and then like something seen from an immensely distant future, when everything in life, good and evil, grief, anger, trouble, joy, will have passed and turned into fond remembrance and forgiveness in an unending quiet. She even sighs as if she were already old, already looking back; then the shock of the arithmetic returns: it is only three years. The hope that carries the last page is not that life will improve, or that poverty will end, but that a day exists — after long life, long sadness, long suffering — from which even these days will be held in that same remembrance and forgiveness. The vision must stay as unparaphrasable in English as it is in Japanese: perhaps old age, perhaps death, perhaps simply time itself, told as a dim picture of “three people” gathered head to head over an endless story, smiling, unmoving, wrapped in quiet.
crux.why: If that distance is clarified into a consolation, a religious promise, or a young wife's determined optimism, the ending collapses into a moral about enduring hardship. The text's force is that she comes back to 'let us work' and 'let us get up early tomorrow' holding something she herself half-says she does not understand, and that the husband can only meet it partway ('…もう少しの間だ').

crux.for_the_english: Domestic detail and visionary abstraction must be allowed the same weight and the same vocabulary. Keep the potato literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything else; keep steam, bowls hidden under the table, the spoon banged down, rice pushed into two mouths at once, breastfeeding at the end, exactly as physical as they are. Do not cut or compress the long domestic opening to 'get to' the meditation, and do not signal the meditation as the important part by changing the music when it arrives.
crux.point: The second crux is that the revelation happens inside, and is continuously interrupted by, an unremarkable supper. Nearly a third of the text is the baby: plump, gripping the table, snatching at everything, so that bowls and pots are moved underneath, leaving only her spoon and small plate; parents smiling helplessly, feeding her and themselves in snatches, forgetting the storm in the noise. The mother's trance is broken twice by the husband's plain 'why are you so quiet?', and what finally answers it is not a confession of the vision but the banal, startling fact: 'it really is only a little while since we married, isn't it.' The story ends not on the vision but on clearing the table, nursing the child asleep, and noticing the weather.
crux.why: A fluent draft will tidy this into an arc — happy family, dark thought, epiphany, renewed resolve — and in doing so will rationalise away what the text actually does, which is to let the eternal and the next morning's early rising sit side by side without commentary. The last line must be allowed to be only 'a storm, isn't it.'

open_questions.question: 「坊や」 is used repeatedly to and of the child, who is stated plainly in p2 to be a girl. Is this a period/familial generic endearment to be neutralised in English ('baby', 'little one'), a deliberate boyish pet name to be kept somehow, or an inconsistency to note? Keeping a literal equivalent risks making English readers misread the child's sex; neutralising loses a period usage.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The child's sex, age and boyish address are part of the period texture; mistranslating any one quietly falsifies the family.

open_questions.question: Who are the three quiet people in the dim picture, heads together over the endless story? The young family transposed into a distant future, an image of all humankind at the end of time, or an intentionally generic vision that should not be resolved even in pronoun and article choices? English will press for definiteness ('the three of them') where the Japanese can leave the figures suspended.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Deciding this decides whether the vision is domestic prophecy or a vision of the whole of life passing, and the text seems to want the second reading to grow out of the first without replacing it.

open_questions.question: Is the coming day of remembrance, forgiveness and 'rest like night' located in old age, after death, or deliberately in neither? Relatedly, how far should '安息' be allowed to sound religious in English ('rest', 'repose', 'peace') without importing a doctrine the text never states?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The consolation's vagueness is its character; too Christian a word makes it a belief, too secular a word makes it mere retirement.

body.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the text does: outside the door, a storm; inside, under a dim lamp hanging by the wall of a narrow room, a young couple — still really young, no wrinkles yet, but with a deep, drowsy weariness already in his hollowed, gentle eyes and in her dark hair and slight shoulders — getting supper with their plump baby daughter. The storm is heard again only twice: once, quietly, in the middle of the mother's silence, and once in the husband's final whisper, when the child has fallen asleep at the breast and everything has gone still. Between those hearings it is forgotten, drowned by the happy bustle of feeding the child. That arc of sound — storm, forgetting, storm — should remain an arc of sound, not be turned into symbolism or pathetic fallacy; the weather does not mirror anyone's feelings, it simply goes on outside, unheard and then heard.

The narration begins with the couple together, their weariness shared, both of them watching the child with all their eyes; then, by way of the potato, it narrows almost imperceptibly into the mother, and for the rest of the text we are mostly inside her drifting attention, which slides — the text keeps saying ふと, いつか, いつとなく, 'before she knew it', 'at some point', 'suddenly' — rather than deciding anything. Who is seeing, and when, is often left soft in the Japanese, and that softness is the medium of the story: present supper, remembered three years, and imagined far future keep soaking into one another, so that she can feel 'as if she had quite grown old' over a life that turns out to have lasted three years. Do not firm these transitions up with signposts ('she realised', 'she imagined', 'years later she would…'). Likewise her silence must stay silence: the husband asks twice why she is quiet, she starts, cannot say it in one breath, smiles 'as if with fond remembrance', and produces only the fact about the three years and, later, the resolve to work. The vision is never reported to him, and the English must not let her reported speech or his answers imply that it has been.

The register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, gentle and slightly formal, but in its own terms plain: the power is in accumulation and recurrence, not in striking phrases. Watch the network of repeated words, which a fluent model will instinctively vary into elegance: 静か (quiet), 遠い (far, distant), 黙って (silently, without speaking), 微笑/笑ひ (the smiles that keep overflowing the parents' faces and fill the faces in the vision), 疲れ・悲しみ・苦しみ (weariness, sadness, suffering, returning in list after list, at the table, in memory, in the vision, in her rallying questions), なつかしみ and 許し (fond remembrance and forgiveness, the paired nouns on which the whole vision turns), 安らかさ (a quiet restfulness that describes the evening, the vision, and the mother's final manner of speaking). These repetitions are the connective tissue; destroying them destroys the text. The sentences should be allowed to run long and loop with 'and… and…' where the Japanese does, and to pool into those slow lists of everything life contains. Shortening them into crisp modern periods would rationalise a consciousness that experiences time as one long, unbroken telling.

Voice and address carry period and class quietly: a poor young household, beef and onions and carrots and potatoes stewed in a dark blue pot, rice steaming from an aluminium pan, things cleared under the table. No ennoblement of the food, no picturesque poverty, and no coarsening either; the husband's speech is rough-edged and warm (「きかない奴だな」, 「さうだなァ」, 「俺たち」), the wife's soft and feminine in the period manner (「…ませんのね」), and the difference between them should be audible in English without dialect costume or archaism. The baby is called 坊や throughout, though she is a girl; see the open questions. What the parents feel for her is rendered physically — the cheek pinched between finger and thumb, rice got into her small red mouth in the gaps of feeding themselves — and the text's tenderness lies in not naming it more grandly than that.

The likely fluent failures are: smoothing the mother's meditation into a tidy inspirational arc with a lesson; making the husband a foil who 'doesn't understand' (he is tired too, he has laboured too, and his 'it won't be much longer' is his own version of the same hope, not a failure of sympathy); explaining the potato; translating the vision's abstractions into richer, more varied, more consoling language than the text permits itself; and tidying away the ending's refusal to end — the table half-cleared, the child asleep mid-feed, a man standing still and murmuring about the weather.
body.say: Reading for Shiraki Shizu's 「晩餐」 (1917): a young, poor couple, worn down after only three years of marriage, eat supper with their baby in a storm. From one mouthful of bad potato the mother drifts into a vision in which their whole life, seen from an immense distance, will turn into fond remembrance and forgiveness; the story stands or falls on keeping that vision as unexplained, repetitive and domestic as the text leaves it — and below are the unresolved questions and the voice I recommend.

voice_takes.label: a
voice_takes.line: Plain, quiet, slightly formal; repetitions and long looping sentences kept, diction kept low so the vision and the potato share one voice. (Recommended.)

voice_takes.label: b
voice_takes.line: Warmer and more lyrical, letting the mother's interior passages rise in cadence above the supper scenes.

voice_takes.label: c
voice_takes.line: Drier and sparser, shorter sentences and modern plainness, letting the strangeness come only from the time-shift itself.

revision.english: Outside the door, grown dark at some point, the sound of violent rain and wind could be heard, a storm.

The parents and child had gathered about the table under the dim electric light hanging against the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. Father and mother were both still truly young. And the child was a plump, round little girl, just able to stand holding on to the table.
notes: Text states plainly the child is a girl; kept literal for the later boya passages where both parents address her as such.

revision.english: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a wrinkle in the face. But in the man's sunken, gentle-looking eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows a dull colour of weariness could be seen. And in the colour of the woman's thick hair and about her slight shoulders a still more sunken deep weariness and a drowsy restfulness could be seen.
The day had ended. The sadness and the suffering of that day were about to flow into the restfulness of the night. And silently smiling, they turned all their eyes upon the child.

The child, standing unsteadily, with fat, round, short hands like balls, was about to stir up the things on the table, leaving not a moment's gap, and far too quickly. So, smiling, they set all the bowls and the teapot and the aluminium pan and the rest under the table. On the table there was left only the small spoon the child held, and a single small plate.
notes: Vessels kept literal for poor-household texture; cleared under the table, not away.

revision.english: But the child gave a noisy cry full of small joy and banged the spoon and the plate down on the table.

"You won't listen, will you." The young father looked hard at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with their rather dark, long lashes, moving quickly and brightly without a moment's pause, as if wondering what was to be done, and then, with a smile over his whole face, lightly pinching the round thrust-out cheek with his finger, he took a large bowl from under the table as if feeling for it and put it into her hand.
notes: I read 彼女の手 as the mother's hand: he hands her the large bowl for her to serve the rice in p8. The Japanese can also read as the child's hand; the passage leaves it soft, so I keep the plain 'her' and flag the doubt for the desk.

revision.english: She served out the hot fresh-cooked rice, with white steam rising thick from the pot, and handed it to him. And her young large eyes too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for an instant, lovely like a little bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring inwardly to herself whatever shall we do with this child, and looking for all the world as if she loved it beyond all help, she said firmly, "Baby," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three of them, as if they had forgotten everything, smiled at one another as if to say what should they do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle, and with smiles and gladness overflowing of themselves on top of it. And in the clattering bustle they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
notes: I keep 坊や as 'Baby' for a girl child, following the bible's policy for period generic use, rather than 'boy'; flagged for editor.
口のうちに独言 is an inward half-uttered murmur rather than spoken address; I keep it as murmuring inwardly to preserve the soft drift toward thought.

revision.english: The young father kept his large red hand spread busily over the table. And his eyes, holding back the smile that welled up in spite of himself because of the child, steadied the child and put a little food into that small red mouth. In the gaps, hurriedly opening a wide mouth, he pushed rice into his own mouth.

The mother, silent and with her head bowed beside the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onions, the carrots and potatoes, stewed in the deep dark-blue pot. And as if to say something, she put into her mouth a potato simmered sweet and soft, and looked at the man's face; but as if she had noticed something, she suddenly closed her mouth and gazed blankly at a far-off place.
notes: Wall phrase is spare in the Japanese; I keep it as place rather than posture, to avoid adding a lean the text does not state.

revision.english: The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty, as if it had frozen, and very tasteless. As if taken by surprise, she silently chewed it over again with her front teeth, but at some point her heart had already sunk down, lonely.
notes: ざくざく kept as gritty rather than mealy or undercooked, to stay literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything else.

revision.english: She remembered the suffering and sadness and weariness of each day. And the flavourless, detached, cold tastelessness of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured to herself the poor, sadness-filled real life since their marriage.
notes: かかりのない kept as detached, not explained into indifference or poverty-symbolism; the detachment happens without commentary.

revision.english: And it seemed like a life dragged on far too long. She suddenly felt as if she herself had quite grown old. And with a distant heart she was quietly remembering the quiet tear-filled days, and the days spent threatened and afraid for material things, and each and every day grieved and suffered through illness. But to her as she remembered now, everything was like a dream. Suffering and sadness too were like a fond dream.
notes: なつかしい rendered as fond to hold the link to なつかしみ and forgiveness later; material want left plain, without glossing into money.

revision.english: And when she came to think of it, it was only about three years of life since their marriage.
Without knowing when, as if her attention had been caught by something, she gazed blankly toward the distance. At some point her quiet heart had been looking at a picture like a vision.
notes: Drift markers kept soft as without knowing when and at some point, without turning them into she realized or she imagined.

revision.english: It was in a faint dim light, and, quiet like that light, three people had drawn together with their heads close, telling a long story. The story seemed to go on and on between them without ever breaking off. And in that story it seemed that everything was told, all the good and evil in the world, and sadness and suffering and anger and trouble, and joy, all of it. But those who spoke and those who listened only went on smiling, quietly and restfully and still, and they did not move at all. With their heads bent and their eyes lowered, only a quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to enfold them there. And there too a deep, deep restfulness showed itself over all of them.

All things in this world, a life, will pass. And only when it has passed, on that day, will everything, all things, change for the first time into fond remembrance and forgiveness. And then they will be forever before a rest like night.

The distant picture lay darkly and quietly at the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely restfulness, that picture could be seen. Young as she was, by herself she gave a lonely hushed sigh, and glancing at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and child, she stayed silent.

"Why are you so quiet?" the man said, looking at the woman's face with a sudden puzzled air. She hurried to say something, but unable to say it in one breath she fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. It was then for the first time that she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.

Yes. That day is there. There is the day when everything will change into fond remembrance and forgiveness, and restfulness. After a long life, and after long sadness, and after long suffering, on the day after that, there is that restful day of fond remembrance and forgiveness. What are the suffering and sadness of each single day? What are the weariness and trouble of each single day? She was smiling before she knew it.
notes: Kept fond remembrance and forgiveness, restfulness, and the lists of sadness, suffering, weariness and trouble in the same plain wording as pp16-17, without varying or lifting them.

revision.english: "Why are you so quiet?" the man said again. She raised her head as if startled, smiling as if with fond remembrance, "It really has been only a little while since we married, hasn't it," she said, as if asking him too to remember, to remember all kinds of things, even the happy things from before their marriage.
notes: Joined pp21-23 as one English paragraph because p21 ends mid-sentence on a comma leading into the p22 speech and the p23 verb that closes it. Rendered natsukashisou ni as as if with fond remembrance to keep the vision's key noun in the same field.

revision.english: "That's so," the man said, looking up too.
"It comes to only three years. But we have been through much hardship, you and I."

"Truly," she said. She lowered her eyes again as if to look at that picture. But at once, "But it is still only three years, isn't it," she said, her eyes shining as if she must tell him of something great, something great she herself did not understand, some great hope.
notes: Joined pp26-27 as one English paragraph because p26 ends mid-sentence leading into the p27 speech. Kept the repetition of great and left hope as hope for nozomi, without explaining what she does not understand.

revision.english: "That's so. Though day by day we are wearied and troubled and made to suffer by one thing and another, two years are past already. In a little while the baby will be walking."
notes: I kept "two years" as written, though p14, p22, p25 and p27 count three years. I did not correct it to three.

revision.english: The man looked at the child standing with the spoon in hand as if at a loss. At once she called out joyfully, "Baby." At the same moment the child gave a loud cry, looking at her mother's face, and banged the spoon down on the table, "uma-uma-uma-uma."
notes: For vocative 坊や to a girl I use Baby throughout, per the bible, to avoid misreading her sex in English. For the babble I transcribe as uma-uma rather than translating it as yummy, to keep it noise rather than speech.

payload.say: Reading for Shiraki Shizu's 「晩餐」 (1917): a young, poor couple, worn down after only three years of marriage, eat supper with their baby in a storm. From one mouthful of bad potato the mother drifts into a vision in which their whole life, seen from an immense distance, will turn into fond remembrance and forgiveness; the story stands or falls on keeping that vision as unexplained, repetitive and domestic as the text leaves it — and below are the unresolved questions and the voice I recommend.

crux.for_the_english: Keep the vision unlocated, unbelabored, and in the same plain diction as the supper. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, a daydream, or a premonition, and do not make the three figures explicitly the couple grown old. Let abstract nouns repeat rather than finding synonyms for them: quiet/rest/peace, nostalgia or fond remembrance, forgiveness, sadness, suffering, weariness. The English will want to vary, explain, and lift these into lyricism; resist that ennoblement.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on a change of temporal distance inside an ordinary mouthful, and on that change not being explained. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless, “as if frozen” — detaches the young mother from the table and lets the three years of her marriage look first like a whole lifetime already lived and then like something seen from an immensely distant future, when everything in life, good and evil, grief, anger, trouble, joy, will have passed and turned into fond remembrance and forgiveness in an unending quiet. She even sighs as if she were already old, already looking back; then the shock of the arithmetic returns: it is only three years. The hope that carries the last page is not that life will improve, or that poverty will end, but that a day exists — after long life, long sadness, long suffering — from which even these days will be held in that same remembrance and forgiveness. The vision must stay as unparaphrasable in English as it is in Japanese: perhaps old age, perhaps death, perhaps simply time itself, told as a dim picture of “three people” gathered head to head over an endless story, smiling, unmoving, wrapped in quiet.
crux.why: If that distance is clarified into a consolation, a religious promise, or a young wife's determined optimism, the ending collapses into a moral about enduring hardship. The text's force is that she comes back to 'let us work' and 'let us get up early tomorrow' holding something she herself half-says she does not understand, and that the husband can only meet it partway ('…もう少しの間だ').

crux.for_the_english: Domestic detail and visionary abstraction must be allowed the same weight and the same vocabulary. Keep the potato literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything else; keep steam, bowls hidden under the table, the spoon banged down, rice pushed into two mouths at once, breastfeeding at the end, exactly as physical as they are. Do not cut or compress the long domestic opening to 'get to' the meditation, and do not signal the meditation as the important part by changing the music when it arrives.
crux.point: The second crux is that the revelation happens inside, and is continuously interrupted by, an unremarkable supper. Nearly a third of the text is the baby: plump, gripping the table, snatching at everything, so that bowls and pots are moved underneath, leaving only her spoon and small plate; parents smiling helplessly, feeding her and themselves in snatches, forgetting the storm in the noise. The mother's trance is broken twice by the husband's plain 'why are you so quiet?', and what finally answers it is not a confession of the vision but the banal, startling fact: 'it really is only a little while since we married, isn't it.' The story ends not on the vision but on clearing the table, nursing the child asleep, and noticing the weather.
crux.why: A fluent draft will tidy this into an arc — happy family, dark thought, epiphany, renewed resolve — and in doing so will rationalise away what the text actually does, which is to let the eternal and the next morning's early rising sit side by side without commentary. The last line must be allowed to be only 'a storm, isn't it.'

crux.why: In p11-14 a badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, coldly flavourless — detaches the mother from supper. In p16-20 that detachment becomes the still picture of three people telling an endless story containing all good, evil, sorrow and anger, while simply smiling; everything will change into なつかしみ and 許し only once life has passed. Author glosses: 卓テーブル, 怜悧れいり, 微笑ほほゑみ, 茫然ぼんやり, 希のぞみ etc. in historical kanaづかひ. Readings fix sense (テーブル as table, ほほゑみ as smile). English cannot show ruby; do not italicise into exoticism. 卓 vs テーブル shift and food vessels (茶碗, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 藍色の深い鍋) carry poor-household period texture to keep concrete.

Ending refuses arc:箸をおいた, resolve to work and rise early, child put to breast falls asleep mid-feed, room goes still, man stands still and whispers 嵐だな. No moral, no consolation gloss. Must allow eternal and next morning to sit side by side; last line only weather, echoing p1 and p19 without symbolism.

motifs.english: Keep one plain English set throughout and repeat, not vary: quiet / quietly for 静か, restful / restfulness for 安らかさ, rest/repose for 安息. Same vocabulary for evening, mother's manner, and vision so table and eternity share language. Do not lift into lyricism or religious peace.
motifs.why: Connective tissue binding supper, memory and vision; fluent English will vary into calm/peaceful/serene/still and destroy network.

motifs.english: Keep far / distant / far-off for 遠い, not remote/removed/estranged. Preserve spatialising of time: future seen through bottom of eyes as distant picture.
motifs.why: Marks mother's detachment: gaze, heart and future all go far. Ordinary usage made deliberate by recurrence; unifies potato moment and vision.

motifs.english: Keep silently / without speaking for 黙って, not wordlessly/tacitly in variation. Her silence is plot: husband asks twice why she is quiet.
motifs.why: From shared smiling silence at table to trance silence to unreported vision; must track as same word.

motifs.english: Keep smile / smiling for 微笑, 笑ひ, ゑみ, ほほゑみ as one field; allow smile overflowed / held back as text has it. Same smiles on parents and on vision figures.
motifs.why: Tenderness and vision share lexis: parents' helpless overflowing smiles and the three figures' continuous quiet smiles. Varying into grin/beam delights would break link.

motifs.english: Keep weariness, sadness, suffering (and trouble/anguish なやみ where present) as fixed equivalents and keep lists long with and…and. Do not compress lists or substitute hardship/pain synonyms.
motifs.why: Recurrence across body, memory and vision is the argument: same burdens at table, in past three years, and inside endless story. Text power is accumulation, not striking phrase.

motifs.english: Keep fond remembrance (or nostalgic fondness if chosen) for なつかしみ and forgiveness for 許し as paired fixed nouns wherever they occur; never paraphrase into nostalgia/pardon/reconciliation variants.
motifs.why: Paired nouns on which whole vision turns; past suffering remembered as なつかしい夢, future all turned into なつかしみと許し. Destroying repetition destroys crux.

motifs.english: Keep storm for 嵐 and sound of rain-wind for 雨風の音 as sound heard, forgotten, heard again. Do not turn into symbolism or pathetic fallacy; weather simply goes on outside.
motifs.why: Frame: p1 heard, p8 unheard through bustle, p19 quietly heard in silence, p38 whispered when still. Must remain arc of sound.

motifs.english: Keep drifting markers as at some point / before she knew it / suddenly for いつか, いつとなく, ふと without firming into she realised / she imagined. Preserve soft transitions where present, memory and future soak into one another.
motifs.why: Medium of story: she slides rather than decides; she feels as if grown old over three years. Signposting would rationalise consciousness that experiences time as unbroken telling.

motifs.english: Keep three years / only three years / only a little while as literal arithmetic shock, repeated plainly. Do not inflate into years of hardship moral.
motifs.why: Felt lifetime versus counted three years is pivot from vision back to resolve to work; repetition carries hope that is not improvement but distant holding.

narration.english_tense: Past as default for supper and memory, allowing the vision's gnomic present-future (p17 過去るであらう…変る事だらう) to stay timeless without shifting whole text into present. Do not use historical present to enliven domestic opening or to signal meditation as important.
narration.frame: Single evening: outside the door a storm; inside a narrow room under a dim lamp hanging by the wall, young parents and plump baby at table for supper. Narration begins jointly on couple watching child, narrows almost imperceptibly via potato into mother, stays mostly inside her drifting attention, returns to shared dialogue and closing tableau of clearing, nursing, stillness, weather.
narration.narrator: Third-person literary narrator, close and gentle, starting omniscient-joint then settling near the mother without explicit interior marking; often leaves who-sees and when soft. Vision never reported to husband; husband's questions and plain answers stay outside it.
narration.person: third person, sliding focus from couple to mother
narration.tense_habits: Japanese mixes てゐた progressive-past and た completion with nonpast/gnomic だらう in reflection; stative weariness and continuing smiles rendered as ongoing states. Historical kana and ruby aid reading but do not change tense. English should allow long looping and… and… sentences and slow lists to pool, not shorten into crisp modern periods.
timeline: p1: outside door, already dark, violent rain-wind, storm
p2-p9: supper begins; baby gripping table snatches so bowls/pots moved underneath leaving spoon and small plate; noisy happy feeding in snatches; storm forgotten
p10-p13: mother serves beef/onion/carrot/potato from dark-blue pot, tastes gritty tasteless potato as if frozen; heart turns lonely, recalls poor sad three married years as dreamlike

p14-p18: arithmetic (only about three years) versus feeling grown old; drifting into dim picture of three quiet people heads together over endless story, smiling unmoving, wrapped in remembrance/forgiveness/rest
p19-p20: husband asks why silent (first time); she starts, cannot say it, hears storm quietly, holds thought that day of remembrance/forgiveness/rest after long life/sadness/suffering exists

p21-p32: husband asks again; she answers only banal startling fact of short marriage and vague great hope; he answers it won't be much longer, child will walk; baby cries うまうま, fed; chopsticks laid down
p33-p38: resolve to work, rise early tomorrow; child put to breast falls asleep cheek to breast; room still; man stands still and whispers storm

bible.say: Hold vision unlocated and diction plain; let eternal and next morning sit side by side. Repeat abstract nouns, do not explain potato or husband, do not end on moral.

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse. Annotate only what sentence cannot give: 坊や usage for a girl, aluminium pot / dark-blue pot period poverty without picturesque gloss, historical kana/ruby where sense depends on gloss, baby babble. Never annotate what context supplies; never use note to resolve vision's three figures or day into heaven/old age/death.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taisho literary prose, gentle slightly formal but plain in its own terms; power in accumulation and recurrence, not striking phrases. Allow long looping sentences and slow lists of everything life contains. Tenderness rendered physically (cheek pinched, rice pushed into two mouths, cheek to breast) not named grandly. Do not ennoble food or poverty, do not coarsen husband's warmth, do not lift vision into lyric consolation.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No surnames or given names in text; do not invent. Keep kin labels as common nouns (father/mother/husband/wife) where narrator uses them. For 坊や do not use Boy/Sonny; use baby / little one with margin note on period generic, pending editor decision, and keep consistent. No Sensei or honorifics to preserve. Name order not applicable.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Nothing kept in Japanese in reading view except defended need: transcribe baby うまうまうまうま as uma-uma with note rather than translating yummy, if editor allows; otherwise plain yummy-yummy babble. Food 御飯 as rice, 茶碗/土瓶/鍋 as bowls/pots in English; do not leave Japanese vessels untranslated.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese uses 『』 for direct speech (きかない奴だな, どうして黙ってるの, 坊や, うまうま, etc.) and embedded thought/独言. Render direct speech in English double quotes, baby babble likewise, with plain dialogue tags. Do not add said-softeners or resolve unattributed speakers where text leaves soft.
style_sheet.register: Narrator: plain gentle literary slightly formal, past-default, long periodic where Japanese loops. Husband speech rough-edged warm masculine colloquial (なァ, 俺たち, 奴, 独言-like strength) without dialect costume or archaism. Wife speech soft feminine period polite (ませんのね, んですものね, ませうね) audible as feminine-polite, not coy. Baby: noise, not lexis.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby gives reading/nuance: 卓テーブル, 怜悧れいり, 微笑ほほゑみ, 茫然ぼんやり, 希のぞみ. Follow gloss sense (table, perspicacious, smile, blankly, hope) in English body; do not italicise or footnote ruby itself unless sense genuinely ambiguous. Italics reserved for emphasis present in sense, not for foreignism.

このファイルは、インターネットの図書館、青空文庫（http://www.aozora.gr.jp/）で作られました。入力、校正、制作にあたったのは、ボランティアの皆さんです。

crux.for_the_english: Keep the vision unlocated, unbelabored, and in the same plain diction as the supper. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, a daydream, or a premonition, and do not make the three figures explicitly the couple grown old. Let abstract nouns repeat rather than finding synonyms for them: quiet/rest/peace, nostalgia or fond remembrance, forgiveness, sadness, suffering, weariness. The English will want to vary, explain, and lift these into lyricism; resist that ennoblement.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on a change of temporal distance inside an ordinary mouthful, and on that change not being explained. A badly cooked potato — hard, gritty, tasteless, “as if frozen” — detaches the young mother from the table and lets the three years of her marriage look first like a whole lifetime already lived and then like something seen from an immensely distant future, when everything in life, good and evil, grief, anger, trouble, joy, will have passed and turned into fond remembrance and forgiveness in an unending quiet. She even sighs as if she were already old, already looking back; then the shock of the arithmetic returns: it is only three years. The hope that carries the last page is not that life will improve, or that poverty will end, but that a day exists — after long life, long sadness, long suffering — from which even these days will be held in that same remembrance and forgiveness. The vision must stay as unparaphrasable in English as it is in Japanese: perhaps old age, perhaps death, perhaps simply time itself, told as a dim picture of “three people” gathered head to head over an endless story, smiling, unmoving, wrapped in quiet.
crux.why: If that distance is clarified into a consolation, a religious promise, or a young wife's determined optimism, the ending collapses into a moral about enduring hardship. The text's force is that she comes back to 'let us work' and 'let us get up early tomorrow' holding something she herself half-says she does not understand, and that the husband can only meet it partway ('…もう少しの間だ').

crux.for_the_english: Domestic detail and visionary abstraction must be allowed the same weight and the same vocabulary. Keep the potato literal and faintly unpleasant before it is anything else; keep steam, bowls hidden under the table, the spoon banged down, rice pushed into two mouths at once, breastfeeding at the end, exactly as physical as they are. Do not cut or compress the long domestic opening to 'get to' the meditation, and do not signal the meditation as the important part by changing the music when it arrives.
crux.point: The second crux is that the revelation happens inside, and is continuously interrupted by, an unremarkable supper. Nearly a third of the text is the baby: plump, gripping the table, snatching at everything, so that bowls and pots are moved underneath, leaving only her spoon and small plate; parents smiling helplessly, feeding her and themselves in snatches, forgetting the storm in the noise. The mother's trance is broken twice by the husband's plain 'why are you so quiet?', and what finally answers it is not a confession of the vision but the banal, startling fact: 'it really is only a little while since we married, isn't it.' The story ends not on the vision but on clearing the table, nursing the child asleep, and noticing the weather.
crux.why: A fluent draft will tidy this into an arc — happy family, dark thought, epiphany, renewed resolve — and in doing so will rationalise away what the text actually does, which is to let the eternal and the next morning's early rising sit side by side without commentary. The last line must be allowed to be only 'a storm, isn't it.'

open_questions.question: 「坊や」 is used repeatedly to and of the child, who is stated plainly in p2 to be a girl. Is this a period/familial generic endearment to be neutralised in English ('baby', 'little one'), a deliberate boyish pet name to be kept somehow, or an inconsistency to note? Keeping a literal equivalent risks making English readers misread the child's sex; neutralising loses a period usage.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The child's sex, age and boyish address are part of the period texture; mistranslating any one quietly falsifies the family.

open_questions.question: Who are the three quiet people in the dim picture, heads together over the endless story? The young family transposed into a distant future, an image of all humankind at the end of time, or an intentionally generic vision that should not be resolved even in pronoun and article choices? English will press for definiteness ('the three of them') where the Japanese can leave the figures suspended.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Deciding this decides whether the vision is domestic prophecy or a vision of the whole of life passing, and the text seems to want the second reading to grow out of the first without replacing it.

open_questions.question: Is the coming day of remembrance, forgiveness and 'rest like night' located in old age, after death, or deliberately in neither? Relatedly, how far should '安息' be allowed to sound religious in English ('rest', 'repose', 'peace') without importing a doctrine the text never states?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The consolation's vagueness is its character; too Christian a word makes it a belief, too secular a word makes it mere retirement.

reading.reading:
Begin with the frame, because the text does: outside the door, a storm; inside, under a dim lamp hanging by the wall of a narrow room, a young couple — still really young, no wrinkles yet, but with a deep, drowsy weariness already in his hollowed, gentle eyes and in her dark hair and slight shoulders — getting supper with their plump baby daughter. The storm is heard again only twice: once, quietly, in the middle of the mother's silence, and once in the husband's final whisper, when the child has fallen asleep at the breast and everything has gone still. Between those hearings it is forgotten, drowned by the happy bustle of feeding the child. That arc of sound — storm, forgetting, storm — should remain an arc of sound, not be turned into symbolism or pathetic fallacy; the weather does not mirror anyone's feelings, it simply goes on outside, unheard and then heard.

The narration begins with the couple together, their weariness shared, both of them watching the child with all their eyes; then, by way of the potato, it narrows almost imperceptibly into the mother, and for the rest of the text we are mostly inside her drifting attention, which slides — the text keeps saying ふと, いつか, いつとなく, 'before she knew it', 'at some point', 'suddenly' — rather than deciding anything. Who is seeing, and when, is often left soft in the Japanese, and that softness is the medium of the story: present supper, remembered three years, and imagined far future keep soaking into one another, so that she can feel 'as if she had quite grown old' over a life that turns out to have lasted three years. Do not firm these transitions up with signposts ('she realised', 'she imagined', 'years later she would…'). Likewise her silence must stay silence: the husband asks twice why she is quiet, she starts, cannot say it in one breath, smiles 'as if with fond remembrance', and produces only the fact about the three years and, later, the resolve to work. The vision is never reported to him, and the English must not let her reported speech or his answers imply that it has been.

The register is Taishō literary prose in historical kana, gentle and slightly formal, but in its own terms plain: the power is in accumulation and recurrence, not in striking phrases. Watch the network of repeated words, which a fluent model will instinctively vary into elegance: 静か (quiet), 遠い (far, distant), 黙って (silently, without speaking), 微笑/笑ひ (the smiles that keep overflowing the parents' faces and fill the faces in the vision), 疲れ・悲しみ・苦しみ (weariness, sadness, suffering, returning in list after list, at the table, in memory, in the vision, in her rallying questions), なつかしみ and 許し (fond remembrance and forgiveness, the paired nouns on which the whole vision turns), 安らかさ (a quiet restfulness that describes the evening, the vision, and the mother's final manner of speaking). These repetitions are the connective tissue; destroying them destroys the text. The sentences should be allowed to run long and loop with 'and… and…' where the Japanese does, and to pool into those slow lists of everything life contains. Shortening them into crisp modern periods would rationalise a consciousness that experiences time as one long, unbroken telling.

Voice and address carry period and class quietly: a poor young household, beef and onions and carrots and potatoes stewed in a dark blue pot, rice steaming from an aluminium pan, things cleared under the table. No ennoblement of the food, no picturesque poverty, and no coarsening either; the husband's speech is rough-edged and warm (「きかない奴だな」, 「さうだなァ」, 「俺たち」), the wife's soft and feminine in the period manner (「…ませんのね」), and the difference between them should be audible in English without dialect costume or archaism. The baby is called 坊や throughout, though she is a girl; see the open questions. What the parents feel for her is rendered physically — the cheek pinched between finger and thumb, rice got into her small red mouth in the gaps of feeding themselves — and the text's tenderness lies in not naming it more grandly than that.

The likely fluent failures are: smoothing the mother's meditation into a tidy inspirational arc with a lesson; making the husband a foil who 'doesn't understand' (he is tired too, he has laboured too, and his 'it won't be much longer' is his own version of the same hope, not a failure of sympathy); explaining the potato; translating the vision's abstractions into richer, more varied, more consoling language than the text permits itself; and tidying away the ending's refusal to end — the table half-cleared, the child asleep mid-feed, a man standing still and murmuring about the weather.
reading.say: Reading for Shiraki Shizu's 「晩餐」 (1917): a young, poor couple, worn down after only three years of marriage, eat supper with their baby in a storm. From one mouthful of bad potato the mother drifts into a vision in which their whole life, seen from an immense distance, will turn into fond remembrance and forgiveness; the story stands or falls on keeping that vision as unexplained, repetitive and domestic as the text leaves it — and below are the unresolved questions and the voice I recommend.

voice_takes.label: a
voice_takes.line: Plain, quiet, slightly formal; repetitions and long looping sentences kept, diction kept low so the vision and the potato share one voice. (Recommended.)

voice_takes.label: b
voice_takes.line: Warmer and more lyrical, letting the mother's interior passages rise in cadence above the supper scenes.

voice_takes.label: c
voice_takes.line: Drier and sparser, shorter sentences and modern plainness, letting the strangeness come only from the time-shift itself.

curious.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The distant picture was reflected darkly and quietly at the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes that picture could be seen, far off in the future, in a lonely restfulness. Young as she was, by herself she gave a lonely hushed sigh, and glancing at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and child, she stayed silent.
curious.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Why are you so silent?" the man said, looking at the woman's face with a sudden puzzled air. She hurried to say something, but unable to say it in one breath she fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the vision-like picture again. It was then for the first time that she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.
curious.ja: 『どうして黙ってるの。』男は、ふと不思議さうに女の顔を見て声をかけた。彼女は、あわてゝなにかを云はうとしたが、一口には何事も云ひかねて黙ってしまふと、再びその眼が遠く走ってしまった。そして彼女は、また幻の絵を見たのだった。彼女は、その時はじめて戸の外の嵐の音を、静かに耳にした。彼女はなにも云はずにゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: Yes. That day is there. There is the day when everything will change into fond remembrance and forgiveness, and restfulness. After a long life, and after long sadness, and after long suffering, on the day after that, there is that restful day of fond remembrance and forgiveness. What of the suffering and sadness of each single day? What of the weariness and trouble of each single day? She was smiling before she knew it.
curious.ja: さうだ。あの日があるのだ。あのすべてがなつかしみと許しと、安らかさに変る日があるのだった。ながい生活の後に、またながい悲しみの後に、またながい苦しみのその後の日に、あの安らかななつかしみと許しの日があるのだ。一日々々の苦しみや悲しみがなんだらう。一日々々の疲れやなやみがなんだらう。彼女はいつとなしに微笑を浮べてゐた。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Why are you so silent?" the man said again. She raised her head as if startled, smiling as if with fond remembrance, "It really has been only a little while since we married, hasn't it," she said, as if asking him too to remember, all kinds of things, even the happy things from before their marriage.

curious.label: house-checked

curious.ja: 『まだ本当にわづかしか経ちませんのね、結婚してから。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.ja: 『さうだなァ。』男も眼を上げて云った。

curious.en: "It comes to only three years. But we've laboured through a lot, you and I."
curious.ja: 『たった三年にしかならないんだな。けれども、俺たちはいろ〳〵苦労したなァ。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Truly," she said. She lowered her eyes again as if to look at that picture. But at once, "But it is still only three years, isn't it," she said, her eyes shining as if she must tell him of something great, something great she herself did not understand, some great hope.
curious.ja: 『本当にね。』彼女は、また眼を伏せてあの絵を見ようとした。が、すぐに、
curious.label: house-checked

curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "That's so. Though day by day one thing and another wears us and troubles us and makes us suffer, two years are gone already. In a little while the baby will be walking."
curious.ja: 『さうだ、一日々々いろ〳〵なことに疲らされなやまされ苦しまされても、二年はもう過ぎたんだからな。もうしばらくすると、坊やも歩るくやうになるんだから。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: The man looked at the child standing with the spoon in hand as if at a loss. At once the mother called out joyfully, "Baby." At the same moment the child, looking at her mother's face, gave a loud cry and banged the spoon down on the table: "uma-uma-uma-uma."
curious.ja: 男は、手持ぶさたのやうにスプーンを持って立ってる子供を見た。彼女は、すぐに嬉しさうに、
curious.label: house-checked

curious.ja: 『坊や。』と大きな声を出した、子供はそれと同時に大きな叫声を上げて、母親の顔を見ながら、
curious.label: house-checked

curious.ja: 『うま〳〵〳〵〳〵。』とスプーンをテーブルにたゝきつけた。
curious.label: house-checked

notes.body: The baby’s sound echoes the Japanese word umai, meaning tasty or yummy. The English keeps it as babble rather than turning it into words.

curious.en: Presently they laid down their chopsticks.
curious.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。

curious.en: "It is only a little while longer," the man said firmly, as if to himself.
curious.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Yes, let's work, shall we," she said, calmly and restfully. Holding the child on her lap, she bared her small nipple and began to nurse.

curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "Come, let us clear away and go to bed. Let us get up early tomorrow, shall we."
curious.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
curious.label: house-checked

curious.label: house-checked

curious.en: "A storm, isn't it," the man whispered, standing still.
curious.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。

student.ja: いつか暗くなった戸の外に、激しい雨風の音がする、嵐だ。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The parents and child had gathered about the table under the dim electric light hanging against the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. student.label: house-checked

student.en: Neither the man nor the woman had yet a wrinkle in the face. But in the man's sunken, gentle eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a dull cast of weariness. And in the woman's thick hair and about her slight shoulders there was an even deeper, sunken weariness and a drowsy restfulness.
student.ja: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The day had ended. The sadness and the suffering of that day were about to flow into the restfulness of the night. And silently smiling, they fixed all their gaze upon the child.
student.ja: 一日が終ったのであった。その日の悲しみも苦しみも、夜の安らかさに流れやうとしてゐるのだった。そして、彼等は黙って微笑しながら、その子供のすべてに瞳を注いだ。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The child, standing unsteadily, with fat, round, short hands like balls, was about to stir up the things on the table, leaving not a moment's gap, and far too quickly. So, smiling, they set all the bowls and the teapot and the aluminium pan and the rest under the table. On the table there was left only the small spoon the child held, and a single small plate.
student.ja: 子供は、あぶなさうに立ちながら、肥えてまるく鞠のやうに短い両手で、すこしのすきまもなく、そしてあまりに早くテーブルの上のものを掻き廻さうとしてゐた。それで彼等は微笑みみながら、すべて茶碗や土瓶、アルミ鍋などを、テーブルの下に置いた。テーブルの上には、わづか子供の持つ小さなスプーンと小皿が一枚残されたばかりであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: But the child gave a noisy cry full of small joy and banged the spoon and the plate down on the table.
student.ja: けれども子供は、さわがしい、小さなよろこびに満ちた叫声を上げて、スプーンと皿をテーブルの上にたゝきつけた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Won't listen, eh?" The young father looked hard at the small round arms and at the child's eyes with their rather dark, long lashes, moving quickly and shrewdly without a moment's pause, as if wondering what was to be done, and then, with a smile over his whole face, lightly pinching the round thrust-out cheek with his finger, he took a large bowl from under the table as if feeling for it and put it in her hand.
student.ja: 『きかない奴だな。』若い父親は、その小さなまるい腕や、敏捷に怜悧にすきもなく動いてる、黒みがちの睫のながい子供の瞳をぢっと見てゐると、どうしたらいゝだらうといふやうに、やがて顔一ぱいな微笑を持って、子供のまるくつき出た頬を指で一寸つまみながら、大きな茶碗をテーブルの下から探すやうにしてとると、彼女の手に渡した。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: She served out the hot fresh-cooked rice, with white steam rising thick from the pot, and handed it to him. And her young large eyes too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, who was never still for an instant, lovely like a little bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring inwardly to herself whatever shall we do with this child, and looking for all the world as if she loved the child helplessly, she said firmly, "Baby," but the smile overflowed from her face, and she looked at the man's face as if asking for help. And the three of them, as if they had forgotten everything, smiled at one another as if to say what should they do for the child. And for the child they set about their meal with a warm bustle, and with smiles and gladness overflowing of themselves on top of it. And in the clattering bustle they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
student.ja: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The young father kept his large red hand spread busily over the table. And his eyes, holding back the smile that welled up in spite of himself because of the child, steadied the child and put a little food into that small red mouth. In the gaps between, he hurriedly opened his mouth wide and pushed rice into it.
student.ja: 若い父親は、彼の赤く大きな片手を忙しくテーブルの上に拡げてゐた。そしてその眼は子供によって仕方がなく湧き出た笑を堪へながら、子供をさゝへて、その小さな赤い口に僅の食物を入れてやった。そのすきに彼は、あわたゞしく大きな口を開けた、彼は彼自身の口のなかに御飯を押し込んだ。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The mother, silent and with her head bowed beside the wall, was serving onto a white plate the beef and onions, the carrots and potatoes, stewed in the deep dark-blue pot. student.ja: 母親は、壁によって黙ってうつむきながら藍色の深い鍋に煮た牛肉と玉葱と、人参とジャガ芋とを白い皿に盛ってゐた。そしてなにか云はうとして、甘く柔かく煮たジャガ芋を口のなかに入れて、男の顔を見たが、彼女はなにかに気がついたやうに、ふと口を閉ぢて茫然と遠い所を見た。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty, as if it had frozen, and very tasteless. As if taken by surprise, she silently chewed it over again with her front teeth, but at some point her heart had already bowed down, lonely.

student.en: She remembered the suffering and sadness and weariness of each day. And the flavourless, detached, cold tastelessness of the potato gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured to herself the poor, sadness-filled real life since their marriage.

student.en: And it seemed like a life dragged on far too long. She suddenly felt as if she herself had quite grown old. And with a distant heart she was quietly remembering the tear-filled days, and the days lived threatened and afraid over material things, and each single day grieved and suffered through in illness. But to her as she remembered now, everything was like a dream. Suffering and sadness too were like a fond dream.

student.en: And when she came to think of it, it was only about three years of life since their marriage.
student.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。

And in that story it seemed that everything was told, all the good and evil in the world, and sadness and suffering and anger and trouble, and joy, all of it. But those who spoke and those who listened only went on smiling, quietly and restfully and still, and they did not move at all. With their heads bent and their eyes lowered, only a quiet fond remembrance and forgiveness seemed to enfold them there. And there too a deep, deep restfulness showed itself over all of them.

student.label: house-checked

student.en: "That's so. Though day by day one thing and another wears us and troubles us and makes us suffer, two years are gone already. In a little while the baby will be walking."
student.ja: 『さうだ、一日々々いろ〳〵なことに疲らされなやまされ苦しまされても、二年はもう過ぎたんだからな。もうしばらくすると、坊やも歩るくやうになるんだから。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The man looked at the child standing with the spoon in hand as if at a loss. At once the mother called out joyfully, "Baby." At the same moment the child, looking at her mother's face, gave a loud cry and banged the spoon down on the table: "uma-uma-uma-uma."
student.ja: 男は、手持ぶさたのやうにスプーンを持って立ってる子供を見た。彼女は、すぐに嬉しさうに、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『坊や。』と大きな声を出した、子供はそれと同時に大きな叫声を上げて、母親の顔を見ながら、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『うま〳〵〳〵〳〵。』とスプーンをテーブルにたゝきつけた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The father hurriedly put rice into the child's mouth.
student.ja: 父親は、あわてゝ子供の口に御飯を入れてやった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Presently they laid down their chopsticks.
student.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "It is only a little while longer," the man said firmly, as if to himself.
student.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes, let's work, shall we," she said, calmly and restfully. Holding the child on her lap, she bared her small nipple and began to nurse.
student.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Come, let us clear away and go to bed. Let us get up early tomorrow, shall we."
student.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Presently the man stood up. When he was about to begin clearing the table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All around had fallen quiet.
student.ja: やがて、男は立ち上った。そしてテーブルを片づけ初めようとした時、もはや子供は乳房に頬をつけて眼を閉ぢてゐた。あたりは静まりかへった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "A storm, isn't it," the man whispered, standing still.
student.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。
